\chapter{Bigger Than, and How Long}
\label{ch:la-bigger-than-and-how-long}
\hlchaptermodality{288}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can compare two things with -ior and quam, and say how long something lasted and how long ago it was.}

Complete LA-R288-bigger-and-how-long: I can compare two things with -ior and quam, and say how long something lasted and how long ago it was.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[longior quam; maior, minor, melior]{longior quam — bigger than, faster than}

\label{lesson:LA-C288-maior-quam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}long\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}fast\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Longus. Celer.})

An experience is often a comparison: the road was longer than you thought, the ship faster than the cart.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -ior and quam}]
Take the stem of the adjective and add \textbf{-ior}, \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}: \emph{long-us}, \textbf{longior}, longer. \textbf{quam} is \textquotedblleft{}than\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Nāvis celerior est quam raeda.} — A ship is faster than a carriage.
\end{quote}

For a neuter word the ending is \textbf{-ius}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Mare altius est quam flūmen.} — The sea is deeper than the river. \textbf{Iter longius erat quam putāvī.} — The journey was longer than I thought.
\end{quote}

\emph{Mare} and \emph{iter} are neuter, so \emph{altius}, \emph{longius}. \emph{Nāvis} is feminine, and \emph{-ior} serves a man or a woman alike: \emph{celerior}.

\emph{Facilis} gives \emph{facilior}, easier. An adjective with a vowel before \emph{-us}, like \emph{idōneus}, usually takes \textbf{magis}, \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}, in front instead: \emph{magis idōneus quam}, more suitable than.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: maior, minor, melior}
Three common adjectives have a comparative of their own, learned whole:

\begin{quote}
\emph{magnus} — \textbf{maior}, bigger. \emph{parvus} — \textbf{minor}, smaller. \emph{bonus}, good — \textbf{melior}, better.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Rōma maior est quam oppidum meum.} — Rome is bigger than my town.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{-ior} ending is inherited: EtymDB 2.1 builds \textbf{maior} from the root of \emph{magnus}, Proto-Indo-European \emph{*méǵh\textsubscript{2}s}, \textquotedblleft{}great\textquotedblright{}, with a comparative ending \emph{*-yos}. \textbf{melior} is traced to a Proto-Indo-European \emph{*melyos}, \textquotedblleft{}better\textquotedblright{}, with no link to \emph{bonus} at all, which is why it has to be learned whole. English took \emph{major}, \emph{minor} and, through French, \emph{ameliorate}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{longus, longior}; \emph{celer, celerior}; \emph{facilis, facilior}
  \item \emph{Nāvis celerior est quam raeda.}
  \item \emph{Mare altius est quam flūmen.}
  \item \emph{maior, minor, melior}
  \item \emph{Rōma maior est quam oppidum meum.}
  \item two things you know, compared with \emph{quam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}longer\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Longior.}}) Say \textquotedblleft{}than\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Quam.}}) Say \textquotedblleft{}bigger\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}smaller\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}better\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Maior, minor, melior.}}) Why is it \emph{altius} with \emph{mare}? (\emph{Mare} is \textbf{neuter}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[abhinc]{abhinc — ago, and for how long}

\label{lesson:LA-C288-abhinc}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}for a long time\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Diū.}) Then \textquotedblleft{}a year\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Annus.})

\emph{Diū} says long without saying how long. Latin can count it out, and the case it counts in is the accusative.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the accusative of how long}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Trēs annōs Rōmae habitāvī.} — I lived in Rome for three years. \textbf{Duās hōrās ambulāvimus.} — We walked for two hours.
\end{quote}

No word for \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{}: the stretch of time stands in the accusative, \emph{annōs}, \emph{hōrās}, and the verb says what filled it. \emph{Duās} is \emph{duo} agreeing with \emph{hōrās}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: abhinc}
\textbf{abhinc} — \textquotedblleft{}ago\textquotedblright{}. It counts back from now, and the count goes in the accusative too:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Abhinc trēs annōs Rōmam vēnī.} — I came to Rome three years ago. \textbf{Abhinc decem diēs nāvis solvit.} — The ship sailed ten days ago.
\end{quote}

Put the two together and a life has a shape: \emph{abhinc} for when it began, the accusative for how long it lasted. Cicero uses \emph{abhinc} with the accusative in his speeches and letters (Lewis \& Short).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{abhinc} is built from \emph{ab}, \textquotedblleft{}from\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{hinc}, \textquotedblleft{}from here, from this point\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), and \emph{hinc} in turn comes from \emph{hīc}, \textquotedblleft{}here\textquotedblright{}. So the word is \textquotedblleft{}from this point\textquotedblright{}, counted backwards into the past. Lewis \& Short note that some early writers also used it forwards, \textquotedblleft{}from now on\textquotedblright{}, a sense that did not last.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{abhinc}
  \item \emph{Trēs annōs Rōmae habitāvī.}
  \item \emph{Abhinc trēs annōs Rōmam vēnī.}
  \item \emph{Duās hōrās ambulāvimus; iter longius erat quam putāvī.}
  \item how long you have lived where you live, and when you came
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{abhinc} mean? (\textbf{Ago.}) Say \textquotedblleft{}three years ago\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Abhinc trēs annōs.}}) Say \textquotedblleft{}for two hours\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Duās hōrās.}}) Which case counts the time? (The \textbf{accusative}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — what it was like}

\label{lesson:LA-R288-bigger-and-how-long}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}the sea is deeper than the river\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{Mare altius est quam flūmen.})
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two chapters, and an experience can be told whole. How it felt, with \emph{eram} and \emph{quod}. What you hope for, with \emph{spērō} and \emph{cupiō}. What was bigger, faster or better, with \emph{-ior}, \emph{quam}, \emph{maior}, \emph{minor} and \emph{melior}. And time counted out: the accusative for how long, \emph{abhinc} for how long ago.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Abhinc duōs annōs Rōmam vēnī. Decem diēs ibi mānsī. Rōma maior erat quam putāvī, et laetus eram.} — I came to Rome two years ago. I stayed there ten days. Rome was bigger than I thought, and I was happy.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Abhinc duōs annōs Rōmam vēnī.}
  \item \emph{Decem diēs ibi mānsī.}
  \item \emph{Rōma maior erat quam putāvī, et laetus eram.}
  \item \emph{Iterum Rōmam vidēre cupiō, et spērō tē valēre.}
  \item a place you have been: when, for how long, and what was bigger or better than you expected
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}two years ago\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Abhinc duōs annōs.}}) Say \textquotedblleft{}for ten days\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Decem diēs.}}) Say \textquotedblleft{}better\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Melior.}}) A woman says \textquotedblleft{}I was happy\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Laeta eram.}})
\end{tcolorbox}
